planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Labuffarosea rain lily naturalizes readily in Gulf South gardens and flowers in flushes after rainfall through the warm season.

directions: Plant bulbs in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Labuffarosea rain lily naturalizes readily in Gulf South gardens and flowers in flushes after rainfall through the warm season. A historic Texas hybrid between Zephyranthes bifida and Z. grandiflora, it produces grassy foliage and funnel-shaped, soft rose-pink flowers that emerge reliably within days of a good rain from late spring through fall, giving the classic rain lily bloom trigger its common name. Long grown as a heirloom pass-along plant across the Gulf South, it multiplies steadily by bulb offsets into dense, long-lived clumps that need dividing only when flowering begins to decline from overcrowding. Plant it along a border edge or in a lawn-adjacent bed where its surprise flushes of bloom after summer thunderstorms can be enjoyed, and leave clumps undisturbed for years for the best display.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Thalia daffodil is one of the more heat-tolerant, reliably perennializing daffodils for warmer climates where many modern hybrids fail to return.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Thalia daffodil is one of the more heat-tolerant, reliably perennializing daffodils for warmer climates where many modern hybrids fail to return. Introduced in 1916 and still widely grown over a century later, this elegant heirloom triandrus-type daffodil produces two to three nodding, pure white, reflexed flowers per stem with a light, sweet fragrance, giving it a graceful, orchid-like poise distinct from the single, forward-facing trumpet of most daffodils. Its old, proven garden performance and good heat tolerance for a daffodil make it one of the more dependable choices for naturalizing in warmer zones where modern large-trumpet hybrids often fail to rebloom reliably. Let foliage yellow and die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer once dormant.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in lean, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun where winters are mild, or in spring after last frost further north, lifting corms for winter storage where the ground freezes; green corn lily needs a dry summer dormancy typical of its South African winter-rainfall habitat.

directions: Plant corms in fall in lean, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun where winters are mild, or in spring after last frost further north, lifting corms for winter storage where the ground freezes; green corn lily needs a dry summer dormancy typical of its South African winter-rainfall habitat. Slender, wiry stems carry loose spikes of unusually colored, translucent, pale sea-green flowers with a dark purple-black central blotch, a striking and unusual flower color rarely seen among common garden bulbs, prized by collectors of unusual South African corms. Native to the winter-rainfall Cape region, it wants moisture during its fall-to-spring growing season and a completely dry, sun-baked rest through summer dormancy, the opposite watering rhythm of most summer-growing garden bulbs. Withhold water once foliage yellows after bloom, and grow in a raised bed, rock garden, or bulb frame where summer moisture can be reliably excluded.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mount Hood daffodil is a classic, widely adapted large-trumpet variety that naturalizes well in most temperate gardens.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mount Hood daffodil is a classic, widely adapted large-trumpet variety that naturalizes well in most temperate gardens. Large, classically shaped flowers open pale creamy-yellow, with the long trumpet fading to pure white as the bloom matures, giving each flower a soft, two-toned transition over its bloom period that is a hallmark of this long-popular heirloom trumpet daffodil. A dependable, vigorous grower since its introduction, it multiplies steadily into large drifts when left undisturbed, making it a favorite for mass plantings, naturalized lawns, and cutting gardens alike. Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering before removing it, and divide crowded clumps every four to five years once dormant in late summer.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; Cretan tulip is a species tulip adapted to rocky Mediterranean hillsides and spreads by stolon into naturalized colonies better than most hybrid tulips.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; Cretan tulip is a species tulip adapted to rocky Mediterranean hillsides and spreads by stolon into naturalized colonies better than most hybrid tulips. Broad, glossy, waxy leaves set off soft lilac-pink flowers with a bold yellow center, opening wide and star-like in full sun, and unlike most modern hybrid tulips bred primarily for cut-flower use, this species tulip spreads by underground stolons into a slowly expanding naturalized patch over years rather than declining after the first season. Native to rocky slopes and cliffs of Crete, it demands sharp drainage and full sun, thriving in a rock garden, gravel bed, or raised bulb bed where its Mediterranean origins are respected. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and avoid summer irrigation, which can rot the bulbs during their dry dormant season.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; Turkestan tulip is one of the earliest species tulips to bloom and naturalizes readily by both offsets and self-sown seed in favorable rock-garden conditions.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; Turkestan tulip is one of the earliest species tulips to bloom and naturalizes readily by both offsets and self-sown seed in favorable rock-garden conditions. Each bulb sends up multiple slender stems bearing several small, star-shaped flowers per stem, creamy white with a golden-yellow base, opening among the very first bulbs of the season, often before crocuses have finished. Native to rocky slopes of Central Asia, it is exceptionally cold-hardy and low-maintenance, multiplying steadily in a rock garden, gravel bed, or naturalized lawn planting where sharp drainage keeps the small bulbs from rotting through summer dormancy. Allow foliage to die back naturally before removing it and avoid summer watering in its dormant season.

planting.note: Plant bulbs after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; two-tone pineapple lily is half-hardy and benefits from a thick winter mulch in zones 7-8 or lifting where winters are more severe.

directions: Plant bulbs after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; two-tone pineapple lily is half-hardy and benefits from a thick winter mulch in zones 7-8 or lifting where winters are more severe. Broad, wavy-edged, strap-shaped leaves with purple-spotted undersides form a bold rosette from which a thick flower spike rises in summer, densely packed with star-shaped, pale green flowers edged in maroon-purple and topped with a tuft of leafy bracts that mimics a pineapple crown, giving the whole plant its distinctive common name. Native to South Africa, it is a long-blooming, low-maintenance summer bulb that provides months of unusual textural and color interest in a border or large container, attracting bees to its abundant small flowers. Water regularly through summer growth, reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall, and mulch heavily over winter or lift and store bulbs in colder zones.
